teach.title: What it does
teach.say: To name the one thing that must hold before the rest is allowed, Latin uses **dummodo + subjunctive (the 'provided that / as long as' condition)**. The verb after *dummodo* goes into the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do), because the thing is not a fact but a requirement: *manē, dummodo taceās* — stay, provided you keep quiet.

check.ask: Tap the verb that names the condition being laid down.

teach.title: The tense: present after a present or future main verb
teach.say: The tense follows the main verb. Present or future in the main clause gives the present subjunctive after *dummodo*: *potest … scrībat*, *exspectābō … veniās*, *dabō … legās*. (A past main verb would give the imperfect, but almost every *dummodo* you meet is about now or about what is to come.)

check.ask: veniās — which tense and mood is it?

teach.title: The negative: dummodo nē
teach.say: To require that something *not* happen, Latin writes *nē*, never *nōn*: **dummodo nē**. The verb is unchanged; *nē* just slips in between. *Manēbō, dummodo nē pater īrātus sit* — I will stay, provided father is not angry.

check.ask: Tap the verb that nē has made negative.

teach.title: modo and dum do the same work
teach.say: *Dummodo* is really *dum* + *modo*, and either half can stand alone with the same meaning and the same subjunctive: *modo taceat* — provided he keeps quiet; *dum cibum accipiat* — as long as he gets food. A bare *modo* or *dum* with a subjunctive verb means 'provided that'.

teach.title: Its two neighbours: dum + indicative, and sī
teach.say: *Dum* with the indicative (the plain statement form) is plain 'while': *dum bibit* is 'while he drinks', *dummodo bibat* is 'provided he drinks' — the verb form is the whole difference. And *sī* with the subjunctive imagines something untrue (*sī tacērēs* — if you were quiet, and you are not), while *dummodo* lays down a requirement that can perfectly well be met.

check.ask: adsit — is it indicative or subjunctive?

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: Write the main clause first, in whatever mood it needs — a statement, an order, or a 'let him …' — then *dummodo* (or *dummodo nē*) and the requirement in the present subjunctive. That is the whole construction.

core.text: The one thing that must hold for the main clause to be true is stated by **dummodo + subjunctive (the 'provided that / as long as' condition)**: *Quidquid vīs, estō — dummodo nīl recitēs!* — be whatever you like, provided you recite nothing. The verb is the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do): present after a present main verb, imperfect after a past one; the negative is *dummodo nē*. *Modo* and *dum* alone can do the same job: *ōderint, dum metuant* — let them hate, as long as they fear. Latin name: *dummodo cum coniūnctīvō*.
English: *provided that*, *as long as*, *so long as*, *only if*: you can go out, *as long as you're back by ten*. A condition with a warning finger raised.
dummodo / modo / dum + subjunctive = provided that; negative dummodo nē.

invented.en: I will wait, as long as you do not come late.

core.text: *sī* + subjunctive imagines something untrue; *dummodo* + subjunctive lays down a real requirement. *Sī tacērēs, manērem* (if you were quiet — you aren't); *manēbō, dummodo taceās* (I'll stay, as long as you keep quiet — and you can).

more.text: Also easy to confuse: *dum* + the present indicative (the plain statement form) is 'while' in a story — *dum gubernātor loquitur* — while the helmsman is speaking, another ship appears (Week 7); *dum / dummodo* + subjunctive is 'provided that'. The verb form tells you which *dum* you have.

The learner's notes have no page on *dummodo*; the three sentences in the texts are all in Weeks 13–14 (Cornelius on the games, Fabia on Sextus's fighting, Martial's *Quidquid vīs, estō*). Allen & Greenough treat it under clauses of proviso: *dum*, *modo*, *dummodo*, and *tantum ut* take the subjunctive, with *nē* as the negative, and often carry a wish along with the condition — *modo nē lūdat* (only let him not play about).

Related uses of *dum* with the subjunctive: 'until' when there is waiting or intention (*exspectā dum veniat* — wait until he comes), and 'while' + subjunctive for background in some writers. With the indicative *dum* is plain 'while' or 'as long as' (*dōnec ego vīvam*, Week 11, is the same idea with *dōnec*).
